newsitem.title: USA: Bond dealers urge ABA to adopt "pay-to-play" ban.
newsitem.headline: Bond dealers urge ABA to adopt "pay-to-play" ban.

text.p: Municipal bond dealers on Tuesday urged the American Bar Association to follow their lead and adopt a voluntary ban on "pay-to-play" by its members at the group's annual meeting in August.

"I understand that at the upcoming meeting in San Francisco, ABA will have before it a resolution addressing pay-to-play," Heather Ruth, president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said. "The dealer community has acted affirmatively to end pay-to-play. I encourage the organized bar to do the same."
Ruth made the remarks in a one-page letter to ABA President Lee Cooper.

She noted that bond dealers four years ago signed a voluntary ban on pay-to-play, which refers to bond professionals who give contributions to elected muni officials in return for a crack at bond business. In all, 50 firms eventually signed the pact, Ruth added.

Then, Ruth said, the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board formally curbed pay-to-play in adopting rule G-37, which bars muni dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from doing business for two years with those governments.
Ruth said bond firms recognized that the muni market's integrity hinges on each dealer maintaining the highest ethical standards.
"This principle is equally applicable to other participants in the offering of municipal securities, including lawyers," Ruth said.
The ABA's Cooper was unavailable for comment.

The Association of the Bar of the City of New York last year adopted a rule similar to the bond dealers' voluntary ban and the New York State Bar Association's ethics panel earlier this month generally approved the rule.
But other bar association's nationwide have rejected it, and several key ABA panel chairmen oppose it.
SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt, who has consistently pressured bond lawyers to adopt a ban, is expected to discuss the issue at a luncheon speech in Philadelphia on Thursday.

"PSA has pointed out that maintaining the integrity of the municipal market falls on the shoulders of all who participate in the market, including the lawyers," Paul Maco, director of SEC's Office of Municipal Securities, said in a telephone interview.
"They deserve to be complimented for making this point to the American Bar Association," he said.
